newsitem.title: USA: New York's falling murder rate reaches milestone.
newsitem.headline: New York's falling murder rate reaches milestone.

text.p: Long infamous for notoriously violent crimes, New York City was safer in 1996 than it has been in years, and for the first time in almost three decades there were fewer than 1,000 murders.

Police records for the calendar year showed steep drops in the number of random killings -- murder by strangers declined twice as much as murder by acquaintances -- and declines in other serious crimes such as rape, robbery and assault.
As of Dec. 30, police reported 978 murders during 1996, the first yearly total below 1,000 since 1968, when there were 986. By comparison, the historic high for murder was 2,245 in 1990.

"We still have a long way to go. The murder rate will still be very high compared with other cities around the world," said Thomas Repetto, head of the Citizens Crime Commission, a private research group.

Many of the 7.3 million people living in the city's five boroughs -- from Mayor Rudolph Giuliani down to ordinary citizens -- were basking at year's end in this relatively new feeling of safety in the Big Apple.

"The number 1,000 is important in the same way as the Dow Jones industrial average breaking through a mark," said Repetto, explaining the significance of the milestone. "It's symbolic, it reflects what most people think is real progress."

Giuliani, a former prosecutor who narrowly won office three years ago on a promise to smash criminals, attributed the record-breaking crime drop to the "cooperation of the entire city" from police officers on the beat, to social workers, teachers and prison officials.
While police officers were fighting crime on the streets, violence in prisons was also down 60 to 70 percent, he said.

"The lives that were saved, the people who were spared from crime were disproportionately poor people, the people who needed help and people living in communities that had the most crime," Giuliani told reporters at a year-end news conference.

The New York City Police Department, the largest police force in the United States, credits a number of strategies for the drop in crime, but mostly its application of what has become known as the "broken windows" theory.
According to the theory, cracking down on people committing minor crimes such as pickpocketing and jumping turnstiles at subway stations prevents them from going on to major crimes such as robbery.
Manhattan, the city's most popular borough for tourists, would likely end the year with about 200 murders, the lowest number since 1960.
Compared with last year, the number of rapes citywide was projected to be down by 4 percent, robberies down by 17 percent and car theft was also down by 17 percent, police statistics showed.
